name: The Goethe Ginkgo of Roedelheim
access: Stands in the grounds of the Petrihaus, which are open to the public only at events of the Foerderverein Petrihaus and on the afternoon of the last Sunday of each month from spring to autumn (per de.wikipedia). Outside those times the tree is not reachable; check the Foerderverein before going.
transport: S-Bahn S3, S4, S5 to Frankfurt-Roedelheim, about 500 m (7 min walk); bus 34 or 72 to Alt-Roedelheim, a few metres away.
story:
In September 1815 Goethe wrote a poem about a single ginkgo leaf, split down the middle and still one leaf, and sent it to Marianne von Willemer with two real ginkgo leaves fixed to the page. Rödelheim would like those leaves to have come from this tree. It has a case, and it does not have proof.

The ginkgo went in around 1750 beside the Petrihaus, in what was then the little County of Solms-Rödelheim. The house later belonged to the banker Georg Brentano, and in September 1814 Goethe was a guest of the Brentano family in Rödelheim. A year later came 'Gingo biloba'. The board at the tree suggests the connection. Wikipedia calls it possible and says the leaves cannot be traced to this tree with certainty, which is where the evidence stops, and so does this page.

The tree needs no poem. The city register gives it about 260 years and 18 metres; the Wikipedia article says over 270 and calls it the oldest ginkgo in Germany, which is that article's claim rather than ours. It stands a few metres south of the Petrihaus, with the Nidda weir just beyond and Brentanopark on the far bank.

The catch is the gate. The grounds open only for events of the Förderverein Petrihaus and on the last Sunday afternoon of each month from spring to autumn, so check before you go. The newest dated photograph we found is from 2017; if you have stood under it since, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one ginkgo in the Petrihaus grounds, about 18 metres tall, with fan-shaped leaves split down the middle. It stands a few metres south of the house, between it and the Nidda weir.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold

verify_notes:
- Official Frankfurt Naturdenkmal entry 021 (register mirrored on de.wikipedia; frankfurt.de page 403s to fetchers). Register: about 260 years old, 18 m tall, next to the Petrihaus in Brentanopark area; called the 'Goethe-Ginkgo'.
- de.wikipedia article 'Ginkgo in Roedelheim': planted about 1750 beside the Petrihaus, then in the County of Solms-Roedelheim; house once owned by banker Georg Brentano. Over 270 years old, described as the oldest ginkgo in Germany, about 18 m high. Protected zone of 10 m around the tree.
- Story: Goethe was guest of the Brentano family in Roedelheim in Sept 1814 and wrote the poem 'Gingo biloba' in 1815 (dated 15 Sept 1815, dedicated to Marianne von Willemer, fair copy decorated with two ginkgo leaves). An information board at the tree suggests the tree may have inspired him; Wikipedia says this is held possible and the leaves cannot be assigned to this tree with certainty. Do not state it as fact (bridge claim).
- Stands south of the Petrihaus, a few metres from it; the Nidda river and weir lie just beyond, Brentanopark on the far bank. Pin is the register coordinate (50.123927, 8.613951), not tree-level confirmed: approximate, small named site (house grounds) with one ginkgo.
- Alive: lifecheck OLD (Commons 2017 Brentano-Park); Commons photo by Frank Behnsen dated 2013-09-29, CC BY-SA 3.0, 1307x1830, shows the tree. Still on the register in the 2025 Amtsblatt list. Flagged: no recent dated sighting found.
- Photo candidate: File:FFM-Roedelheim Ginkgo biloba 02.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, Frank Behnsen). Also Wikidata Q15111648.
- No age basis other than the register and Wikipedia; no girth found.

name: The Paradieseiche of Sachsenhausen

location.address: Corner of Oberer Schafhofweg and Saechsenhaeuser Landwehrweg, 60599 Frankfurt am Main

access: Free. Stands at a street corner on the edge of the Stadtwald; visible from the public roads. Protected zone of 20 m around the tree.
transport: Not verified; Sachsenhausen-Sued, roughly 2 km south of the Sachsenhausen centre. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
story:
Frankfurt protects this oak for two reasons, and one of them is a beetle. The city's register entry 035 lists the tree's rare, striking form, and then adds that it is habitat for the stag beetle, a protected species that depends on old oaks.

It was not always the main event. The city's own description says it was once just one oak among many in the Stadtwald, the city forest on Frankfurt's south side, and is now a solitary tree that shapes the landscape around it. Somewhere along the way people started calling it the Paradieseiche, the Paradise Oak. The city records the nickname and does not explain it. If you know where it comes from, tell us.

The numbers are the city's own. It is 140 to 160 years old, which puts it in the second half of the 19th century, with a trunk about 4.2 metres round, a crown about 20 metres across and a height of 25 metres. For an oak of that age, that is a lot of tree.

It stands at the corner of Oberer Schafhofweg and Sachsenhäuser Landwehrweg, on the forest edge in Sachsenhausen-Süd, and you see it from the road. There is nothing to pay and no gate, and a protected zone of 20 metres runs around the trunk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big oak at the street corner, about 25 metres tall with a trunk 4.2 metres round, standing apart from the forest. It stands where Oberer Schafhofweg meets Sachsenhäuser Landwehrweg.
verify_notes:
- Official Frankfurt Naturdenkmal entry 035. City page (read via Wayback snapshot, frankfurt.de itself is Cloudflare-blocked): Quercus robur, age 140 to 160 years, girth about 4.2 m, crown about 20 m, height 25 m, location corner 'Oberer Schafhofweg' / 'Saechsenhaeuser Landwehrweg', protected radius 20 m. The register mirror on de.wikipedia agrees (4.20 m, 25 m).
- Official text: once just one oak among many in the city forest, now a landscape-shaping solitary tree sometimes nicknamed 'Paradieseiche'. Protected for its rare, striking form in the city area and because it is habitat for the protected stag beetle (Hirschkaefer).
- Pin: register coordinate (50.085418, 8.676653) matches the stated street corner; not tree-level confirmed, so approximate. Commons photo (CC BY-SA 4.0, user Fernando Ferkelkraut, 2020-07-19, 3648x4815) shows the tree; not geotagged.
- Alive: Commons photo dated 2020-07-19; lifecheck found RECENT 2024-05 iNaturalist observation at the spot but it records a ground plant, so it only proves the place was visited. Still listed on the 2025 register. Flagged only by thin dated evidence of the trunk itself; deliver unflagged because the register is current.
- Age is the city's own estimate, 140 to 160 years; no bridge to any planting.

name: The Schwanheim Old Oaks

location.address: Alteichen-Pfad, Schwanheimer Wald, 60529 Frankfurt am Main

access: Free. Open forest path (the Alteichen-Pfad, part of the Frankfurt GruenGuertel) through the group, with information stelae.
transport: Not verified; Schwanheim in the southwest of Frankfurt, reached on foot from the district through the Schwanheimer Wald. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
story:
Until the 1920s, pigs were driven into this wood to feed under these oaks, and in the Middle Ages sheep, goats, horses and cattle grazed here too. That is the whole explanation for the place: about thirty pedunculate oaks that grew up on open, grazed ground rather than packed into a forest, which is what wood-pasture means.

Germany was once full of it. From the 18th century most of it was replaced with spruce plantations, and what survived became a favourite subject for the painters of the Kronberg colony. One of them, Fritz Wucherer, painted 'Bei den Schwanheimer Eichen' in 1899, showing a conspicuous oak whose trunk forks in two. A large reproduction stands on the path, so you can compare the painting with the trees.

How old they are depends on which official text you read. The city's own page says up to 500 years; the register as mirrored on German Wikipedia says 600 to 1,000. Several centuries is as far as the sources agree. They are only 12 to 16 metres tall, and the trunks average about 2.75 metres round.

The thickest carries thumb-thick galleries bored by the great capricorn beetle, and woodpeckers come for the larvae. Not all the news is good. For some years the oaks have been suffering from climate change, their crowns thinning and branches dying, and some of the group is already dead wood.

The Alteichen-Pfad, part of Frankfurt's GrünGürtel, runs through the group. It is open forest, and free.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the group of about thirty old oaks along the Alteichen-Pfad, with information stelae and a large reproduction of Wucherer's 1899 painting beside the path. They stand in the Schwanheimer Wald.
verify_notes:
- Official Frankfurt Naturdenkmal entry 030, a group of about 30 pedunculate oaks (ensemble: one trail, one place to stand). City page (via Wayback): about 30 Stieleichen, age up to 500 years, mean girth about 2.75 m, height 12 to 16 m. de.wikipedia register mirror says 'between 600 and 1000 years': SOURCES CONFLICT on age (city page up to 500, Wikipedia register 600 to 1000); writer should say 'several centuries' and not pick one. age_min/max here follow the city's own page.
- Story: former wood-pasture (Huteeichen); until the 1920s pigs were herded under them, in the Middle Ages also sheep, goats, horses and cattle. Open wood-pasture was once common in Germany, replaced by spruce plantations from the 18th century, which is why it was a favourite motif of the Kronberg painters' colony. Painter Fritz Wucherer made 'Bei den Schwanheimer Eichen' in 1899 showing a conspicuous oak with a forked trunk (Zwiesel); a large reproduction stands on the path so you can compare it with the real trees.
- The thickest oak shows thumb-thick feeding galleries of the great capricorn beetle (Eichen-Heldbockkaefer), eaten by woodpeckers.
- The oaks have suffered from climate change for some years: crowns losing leaves, many branches dying.
- Pin: register coordinate (50.0823, 8.5898) for the group; Commons has dozens of geotagged photos of the oaks dated 2025-07-11 within 60 m of it (e.g. File:Schwanheimer Alteichen SAC Schwanheimer Wald 2025-07-11 39.jpg at 50.08232, 8.58995), so the group is alive and the location of the group is confirmed; individual trunks are not. Dead wood photos 'FFM-Schwanheim Eichen-Totholz' exist, some trees are dead.
- Photo candidates: File:FFM Schwanheimer Alteichen 07-2012 02.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, Frank Behnsen, 2012-07-22) and the 2025-07-11 series (check licence on viewing pass).
- Girth 275 cm is the city's AVERAGE over the group, not one trunk.

name: The Peace Oak of Sossenheim
access: Free. Stands on the Wiesenfeldweg at the southern edge of Sossenheim, between housing and allotment gardens; seen from the public way. Protected zone of 20 m.
transport: Not verified; southern edge of Sossenheim. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
story:
Lightning once split this oak from its crown to its roots, and it is still standing. The crack is part of the city's own description of the tree, entry 022 on Frankfurt's register of natural monuments.

It was planted in 1871 to mark the peace that ended the Franco-Prussian War, which makes it a Friedenseiche, a peace oak, put in the ground in the same year the German Empire was proclaimed. That gives it something most old trees lack: a known birthday, and an age of about 150 years that nobody had to estimate.

It also stands on an old line. Sossenheim was a village before it was part of Frankfurt, and until about 1800 it was closed in by a Haingraben, a fence and hedge with a ditch along it. The oak stands where the village edge used to be. Today that edge is the Wiesenfeldweg, between housing and allotment gardens, and the tree has outlasted both the Empire it was planted under and the peace it was planted for.

It is 4.60 metres round and about 18 metres tall, a broad trunk for a century and a half. The city does not say whether the lightning crack is weakening it, and we will not guess. The newest dated photograph we have found is from 2020; if you have walked past since, tell us how it looks.

It is free, and seen from the public way at the southern edge of Sossenheim.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.60 metres round, and the lightning crack the city records from crown to roots. It stands on the Wiesenfeldweg at the southern edge of Sossenheim, between the houses and the allotments.
verify_notes:
- Official Frankfurt Naturdenkmal entry 022. City page (via Wayback): Quercus robur, over 140 years, girth 4.60 m, height about 18 m, location Wiesenfeldweg in the south of Sossenheim between housing and allotments, protected radius 20 m. Register mirror: planted 1871, 18 m, girth 4.60 m.
- Story: planted to mark the peace after the Franco-Prussian War in 1871 (city page); this is the dating basis, a documented planting for this tree, hence age about 150 years. Once struck by lightning, which left a crack from crown to roots. It stands where the village edge used to be; until about 1800 Sossenheim was ringed by a 'Haingraben' (fence-and-hedge with ditch).
- Pin: register coordinate 50.118534, 8.568319 and OpenStreetMap natural=tree node 5365412440 ('Sossenheimer Friedenseiche', Quercus robur, start_date 1871, height 18, denotation natural_monument) at 50.1185545, 8.5682546 lie about 5 m apart: tree-level, confirmed.
- Alive: lifecheck OLD (Commons 2020-06-13); Commons photos by Karsten Ratzke dated 2016-07-01 (CC0, 4416x6064, File:Sossenheimer Friedenseiche.jpg). OSM node maintained. No sighting newer than 2020 found, flagged.
- Lightning crack is a hazard note; city page does not say whether the tree is declining.

name: The Castle Square Oak of Hoechst

location.address: Hoechster Schlossplatz, in front of the Zollhaus, 65929 Frankfurt am Main

access: Free. On the public Hoechster Schlossplatz in the old town, in front of the Zollhaus entrance; a wooden bench rings the trunk.
transport: Not verified; Hoechst old town, beside the Hoechst Schloss on the Main. Check RMV (Hoechst S-Bahn is in the district).
story:
Frankfurt's register entry for this oak says it is still fairly young and has not reached its full size, which is a candid thing to write into the document that protects it. It is over 150 years old, about 13 metres tall and 2.6 metres round. None of that is a record. What it has is the square.

The Höchster Schlossplatz sits in the tight old town of Höchst, beside the castle on the Main, and the city's own text calls the oak the formative centre of the place. Its crown spreads about 21 metres, wider than the tree is tall, over a square closed in by old buildings. A wooden bench runs in a ring around the trunk, which tells you what the square thinks the tree is for.

It stands in front of the entrance to the Zollhaus, and it was already here when Höchst was still a town of its own. Frankfurt only absorbed it in 1928, so this oak has been the middle of the square under two different town halls. Today the city protects it as natural monument 024, with a zone of ten metres around the trunk.

So come for the place rather than the measurements. There is nothing to pay and nothing to find: walk into the square, look for the bench, and sit on it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wooden bench built in a ring around its trunk. It stands on the Höchster Schlossplatz, in front of the entrance to the Zollhaus.
verify_notes:
- Official Frankfurt Naturdenkmal entry 024. City page (via Wayback): Quercus robur, over 150 years, girth about 2.6 m, height about 13 m, crown about 21 m, location in front of the Zollhaus entrance on the Schlossplatz in Hoechst, protected radius 10 m. Register mirror agrees (over 150 years, 13 m).
- Official text: the trunk is ringed by a wooden bench; the tree is still fairly young and has not reached full size; in the tight old-town buildings it is the formative centre of the place. Age is the city's 'over 150 years' only; age_max 180 is a loose band, do not print a figure beyond 'over 150 years'. Girth is modest (2.6 m): remarkable for its setting, not for size. The writer should not overclaim.
- Pin: register coordinate with 4 decimals (50.0987, 8.54776), approximate; the square is a small named site and the oak is the one with the bench in front of the Zollhaus.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT 2026-05-09 (iNaturalist observation 365859537 at the spot, may be another plant); Commons photo by Steinschneider dated 2018-04-29, CC BY-SA 4.0, 5184x3888 shows it. Register current (2025).

name: The Senckenberg Yew

location.address: Palmengarten, north-eastern edge, south of the playground and north of a greenhouse

verified_sources: https://www.palmengarten.de/fileadmin/user_upload/Dokumente/Sehenswerte_Gehoelze_Palmengarten_2022.pdf (cited by de.wikipedia for the position; PDF text not read by this pass)
access: Paid entry to the Palmengarten: regular day ticket 9 euro (10 euro from 16 October 2026 to 7 February 2027). Open daily, March to October 9:00 to 19:00, November to February 9:00 to 16:00 (hours as verified for frk_003, same garden).
transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance
story:
In 1907 two steam rollers dragged this yew three and a half kilometres across Frankfurt, its roots boxed in a block of earth that weighed about 45 tonnes.

For three centuries it had grown in the garden at the Eschenheimer Turm that the physician Johann Christian Senckenberg bought in 1766: his botanical garden, with his hospital and anatomy beside it and later a library and museum. When the Senckenberg foundation sold the site in 1907, its administrators asked for two things to be kept. One was Senckenberg's tomb. The other was this tree.

Keeping the tree took three years. On the advice of an English specialist in moving old trees, the main roots were trenched and cut back so that new ones would form at the stumps. The rootball came out 4.5 metres square and 2 metres deep, was boxed in timber and set on rollers, and between late May and June it crossed the city. Philipp Holzmann's firm did the work, the public was asked for money and the city council paid in. Frankfurt's city history institute says no tree that old and that big had ever been moved so far.

Roughly 400 years is the best figure. The institute put it at about 300 at the time of the move, and local tradition has it planted before the Thirty Years War. German Wikipedia counts it among the oldest yews in the country.

It joined the Palmengarten in 1960, so seeing it costs a ticket.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the information boards at the tree, which tell the story of its 1907 move. It stands at the north-eastern edge of the Palmengarten, south of the playground and north of a greenhouse.
verify_notes: Position is the Wikipedia/Wikidata coordinate (50.12538, 8.65705), described by de.wikipedia (citing the Palmengarten's own 'Sehenswerte Gehoelze' guide and the information boards at the tree) as the north-eastern edge of the Palmengarten, south of a playground, north of a greenhouse. Garden is a walk-through park, so no location_site; approximate. About 130 m from frk_002 (Dawn Redwood, Botanical Garden), more than 250 m from frk_004. Not a Naturdenkmal on the 2025 register. AGE: de.wikipedia says about 400 years and one of the oldest yews in Germany; the Institut fuer Stadtgeschichte newsletter 8 (June 2007) says the tree was already about 300 years old in 1907 and that local tradition has it planted before the Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648). 300 years in 1907 gives roughly 420 now; both agree on 'roughly 400', recorded broad. HEIGHT: about 12 m at the 1907 move (de.wikipedia); a historical figure, not a current measurement, so no height_m. STORY FACTS: the yew stood in the garden Johann Christian Senckenberg bought in 1766 at the Eschenheimer Turm (his old botanical garden, with hospital, anatomy and later library and museum). In 1907 the Senckenberg foundation sold the site; the administrators wanted two things kept, Senckenberg's tomb and this yew. Roots were trenched and cut three years in advance (an English specialist in moving old trees advised cutting the main roots to length so new roots would form at the stumps). Rootball 4.50 m square and 2 m deep, boxed in timber, estimated 900 Zentner (de.wikipedia: about 45 tonnes), on rollers, hauled by two steam rollers over about 3.5 km between 22 May and June 1907 (preparations from late April to 17 May; contractor Philipp Holzmann; public appeal for funds, city council contributed). The newsletter says no tree of that age and size had ever been moved that far. It was a Frankfurt sensation in 1907. Integrated into the Palmengarten in 1960. Source of the transport figures: Institut fuer Stadtgeschichte newsletter 8 and de.wikipedia (Natur und Museum 137, 2007, pp. 236-237 cited there). PHOTO: none usable; the only Commons file is the 1907 scan (SenckenbergEibe.jpg, a scan of a photograph of the 1907 move, not the living tree and not eligible). Photo candidate to look for on site: none named. ALIVE: iNaturalist observation 2026-04-26 near the pin; Palmengarten 2022 guide lists it.

name: The Red Oak of the Ostpark
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 025, Roteiche im Ostpark, citing Amtsblatt fuer Frankfurt am Main Nr. 44/2025, 28 Oct 2025, pp. 776-789 (Naturdenkmal overview, object sheets, deleted list))
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roteiche,_3,_Ostend,_Frankfurt_am_Main.jpg (GeorgDerReisende, CC BY-SA 4.0, taken 2025-11-13: red oak at the north-eastern end of the Ostpark)

official_register.name: Stadt Frankfurt am Main Naturdenkmal register (Amtsblatt Nr. 44/2025)

access: Free. Public city park (Ostpark); opening hours not verified.
transport: Not verified; Ostpark in Ostend, check RMV for the nearest stop.
story:
In October 2025 Frankfurt went through its register of natural monuments and struck off a long list of entries. This red oak stayed. The revised register keeps it as natural monument 025 and gives its reasons in three words: rarity, character and beauty.

Those three words are close to everything on record. The register lists no age, no girth and no height for it, and no source we have found says when it was planted or by whom. What can be said is short. It is a northern red oak, a species from eastern North America, standing at the north-eastern end of the Ostpark in Ostend. Somebody logged it nearby in May 2024, and a photograph taken in November 2025 shows it at that end of the park, still standing after the cull of the register.

The species is the reason to come in autumn. Red oaks were planted across Europe for the colour their leaves turn, a rich red that Frankfurt's native oaks do not manage, and the lobes of each leaf end in fine bristles where a pedunculate oak's are rounded.

The Ostpark is a free public city park. The pin is approximate, so head for the park's north-eastern end and look for the oak with the pointed leaves. Nobody has published how old or how big this tree is. If you have stood under it with a tape measure, or know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its leaves, every lobe ending in a bristle tip where native oaks are rounded, and by their red in autumn. It stands at the north-eastern end of the Ostpark.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the leaves turn a rich red

verify_notes: REGISTER ONLY plus a photograph: ND 025 on the revised Naturdenkmal register of October 2025 (Seltenheit, Eigenart, Schoenheit). The register mirror holds no description, girth or height for this entry and the frankfurt.de object page 403s (Cloudflare); Amtsblatt PDF 403s; no Wayback copy. No age, girth or height recorded: do not invent. Position is the register coordinate; the Commons photo caption ('north-eastern end of the Ostpark') agrees with it but the file carries no geotag, so approximate. Alive: photograph of 13 Nov 2025 and the tree surviving the 2025 register revision (many entries were deleted), iNaturalist observation May 2024 nearby. Why it is on the register: Seltenheit, Eigenart, Schoenheit per the register; a red oak, a North American species. No source states anything more about the tree itself. name: The Cemetery Lindens of Nieder-Erlenbach
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 036; description 'Drei ueber 100 Jahre alte Winterlinden auf dem Friedhof von Nieder-Erlenbach', citing the frankfurt.de object page, Amtsblatt fuer Frankfurt am Main Nr. 44/2025, 28 Oct 2025, pp. 776-789 (Naturdenkmal overview, object sheets, deleted list))
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lindengruppe_in_Nieder-Erlenbach,_Naturdenkmal.jpg (Fernando Ferkelkraut, CC BY-SA 4.0, taken 2020-06-07: two Winterlinden at the cemetery entrance)

official_register.name: Stadt Frankfurt am Main Naturdenkmal register (Amtsblatt Nr. 44/2025)

access: Free. Village cemetery, open to visitors (cemetery gate; no admission). Opening hours not verified.
transport: Not verified; far-north district of Frankfurt, roughly 15 km from the centre. Check RMV for bus connections to Nieder-Erlenbach.
story:
Frankfurt's register says there are three small-leaved limes at this cemetery. The newest photograph we have found, taken at the entrance in June 2020, shows two. Either the third stands out of the frame or it has gone, and nothing we have read settles which. If you go, count them and tell us.

The register line itself is plain: three Winterlinden over 100 years old on the cemetery of Nieder-Erlenbach. They are natural monument 036, protected for rarity, character and beauty, and they came through the October 2025 revision of the register, which removed many other entries. So as recently as 2025 the city still thought the group worth keeping.

That is all that is written down. No girth, no height, and an age that is a floor rather than a figure: over a century, and nobody has published a closer date, or who planted them by the gate.

Small-leaved limes flower late, in July, after the other limes have finished. That is the month to come, when the entrance smells of them.

Nieder-Erlenbach is in Frankfurt's far north, about 15 kilometres from the centre. The cemetery is free to enter. About 500 metres east, in front of the Protestant church's community house, stands a protected oak 4.55 metres round, so the two make a short village walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the limes at the cemetery entrance: the register counts three, a 2020 photograph shows two. They stand at the gate of the Nieder-Erlenbach cemetery.

best_time.label: July, when the limes flower late and scent the cemetery gate

verify_notes: Register ND 036 (Seltenheit, Eigenart, Schoenheit), listed after the October 2025 revision. Register text: three Winterlinden over 100 years old. The Commons photo (June 2020) captions two limes at the cemetery entrance; count conflict three (register) versus two visible in the photo, recorded rather than smoothed. Stands on a small named site taken in at one glance: tell them apart by position at the cemetery entrance/gate (from sources only). No girth or height available (frankfurt.de page 403). Age 'over 100 years' is the register's; recorded broad as 100 to 150, derived from nothing but that line. Alive: on the 2025 register after a revision that deleted many entries; last photograph 2020 (lifecheck OLD), so flagged. Photo candidate (not hunted): Commons 'Lindengruppe in Nieder-Erlenbach, Naturdenkmal.jpg', CC BY-SA 4.0. Pairs with frk_015 (about 520 m east) as a short village walk.

name: The Oak on An der Bleiche, Nieder-Erlenbach

location.address: An der Bleiche 8, in front of the Gemeindehaus of the Protestant church, Frankfurt-Nieder-Erlenbach

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 037: over 100 years old, about 4.55 m trunk circumference, on the grounds of the evangelical regional association, citing the frankfurt.de object page; Amtsblatt fuer Frankfurt am Main Nr. 44/2025, 28 Oct 2025, pp. 776-789 (Naturdenkmal overview, object sheets, deleted list))

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ND_Stieleiche,_1,_Nieder-Erlenbach,_Frankfurt_am_Main.jpg (GeorgDerReisende, CC BY-SA 4.0, taken 2021-01-29: Naturdenkmal oak in front of the church community house, An der Bleiche 8)

official_register.name: Stadt Frankfurt am Main Naturdenkmal register (Amtsblatt Nr. 44/2025)

access: View-only from the public street: the tree stands in front of the church community house on the grounds of the Protestant regional association. Free to see from An der Bleiche; no source says the grounds are open, so the pin is the viewing place at the street.
transport: Not verified; far-north district of Frankfurt, roughly 15 km from the centre. Check RMV for bus connections to Nieder-Erlenbach.
story:
This oak is 4.55 metres round, and the document that protects it will only say it is over 100 years old. That gap between the tape measure and the date is the most interesting thing on record about it.

It is natural monument 037 on Frankfurt's register, listed for its character and beauty, and it was kept when the city revised the register in October 2025 and deleted many other entries. The register gives the girth and the floor of the age and nothing else: no height, no planting date, no story. Nobody has published a closer figure, and we will not invent one from the girth.

It stands in front of the community house of the Protestant church at An der Bleiche 8 in Nieder-Erlenbach, on ground that belongs to the Protestant regional association. No source we have found says those grounds are open, so treat it as a tree to look at from the street, which is where the pin is. The newest photograph we know of is from January 2021. If you pass it, or know when it was planted, tell us.

Nieder-Erlenbach is a village district in Frankfurt's far north, about 15 kilometres from the centre. The protected cemetery limes are about 500 metres west, which makes the pair a short walk through the village.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.55 metres round, the big oak in front of the church community house. It stands at An der Bleiche 8, seen from the street.

story:
By the register's figures this horse chestnut put on more than five metres of trunk in about 110 years. Frankfurt lists it at 5.30 metres round and 17 metres tall, and that is a great deal of girth for the age. Both numbers come from the same city entry and we print them as the city does, but one of them may be generous. If you know which, tell us.

It is natural monument 032, and the register gives three reasons for keeping it: its character, its beauty and what the register calls landeskundliche Gründe, roughly reasons of regional history and geography. The entry does not say what that history is. It came through the October 2025 revision of the register, which deleted many other trees, and a photograph from June 2020 shows it standing at Am Schäferköppel, on the northern edge of Nieder-Erlenbach, the northernmost district of Frankfurt and about 20 kilometres from the centre.

How you reach it is the thin part. Nothing we have read says whether it stands on the edge of a public path or in a field, so the pin is the register's coordinate and nothing finer. If the ground turns out to be farmland, look at it from the road and leave the field alone.

Come in May, when horse chestnuts hold white candles upright over the whole crown. The cemetery limes and the oak on An der Bleiche are about two kilometres south, in the village.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the horse chestnut with a trunk 5.30 metres round and a crown about 17 metres high. It stands at Am Schäferköppel, on the northern edge of Nieder-Erlenbach.

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown

name: The August Reiss Oak of Offenbach

location.address: Offenbach city forest, on the forest route near the Pechschneise, about 300 m east of the road to Dietzenbach, Offenbach am Main (day trip from Frankfurt)

verified_sources: https://www.offenbach.de/waldroute?loc=en (City of Offenbach forest route, stop 10 'August Reiss oak': planted around 1590, over 40 m high, trunk almost 2 m in diameter, oldest tree in Offenbach, natural monument)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Offenbach_am_Main (cites Wittenberger and Schablitzki, Die Naturdenkmale und Landschaftsschutzgebiete von Offenbach am Main, Offenbacher Verein fuer Naturkunde for the Magistrat, 1979: planted 1590, about 40 m high, 300 m east of the Dietzenbach road at the Pechschneise)
access: Free. Stands beside a public forest path on the city's own signed Waldroute (the oak is stop 10, 'on the path over the bridge near the Pechschneise'); the city page says it is overgrown with bushes. Forest, no gate.
transport: Offenbach am Main is S-Bahn-connected to Frankfurt (travel time not verified); the oak is a forest walk roughly 3 km south of the Offenbach centre. Nearest stop not verified; check RMV.
story:
This oak was planted around 1590, which makes it older than the Thirty Years War and, by the City of Offenbach's own count, the oldest tree in Offenbach. The city's forest route and a 1979 survey of its natural monuments agree on the date.

It is also tall: over 40 metres by the city, about 40 by the survey, near the top of what a pedunculate oak reaches, and nobody has published a newer measurement. The trunk is almost two metres across. That works out at roughly six metres round, which is our arithmetic from the diameter, not anyone's tape.

The name honours August Reiss, 1844 to 1929, forestry inspector of the princely Isenburg forests from 1874 to 1927. When he started, the oak was nearly three hundred.

The oak is stop 10 on Offenbach's signed Waldroute, on the path over the bridge near the Pechschneise, about 300 metres east of the road to Dietzenbach. The city warns that bushes have grown up around it. The forest is free, with no gate. The list of Offenbach's natural monuments records two other oaks as gone, one fallen and one felled in 2019, and the newest photograph of this one is from August 2020; if you have seen it since, tell us.

Offenbach is its own city, an S-Bahn ride from Frankfurt, and the oak is a forest walk of about three kilometres south of its centre. Check RMV for the journey.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 40 metres, and the bushes grown up round its trunk. It stands at stop 10 of the Waldroute, by the path over the bridge near the Pechschneise.
verify_notes: Two sources agree: the City of Offenbach's own forest-route page and the 1979 naturalist-society survey for the city (via the Wikipedia ND list). Age: both say planted around 1590, which gives about 435 years; this is a documented planting date for this specimen per both sources, recorded broad (400 to 450). Height about 40 m (city page 'over 40 m', 1979 survey 'about 40 m'); a 40 m pedunculate oak is on the high end, sanity-checked as plausible for a 435-year forest oak but flagged. Girth: the city page gives 'trunk almost 2 m in diameter'; girth_cm 600 is diameter times pi rounded down (about 6.1 m), a derived figure, not a measured circumference. Named after August Reiss (1844 to 1929), forestry inspector of the Fuerstlich Isenburgische Waldungen between 1874 and 1927 (city page). The city calls it the oldest tree in Offenbach; designated Naturdenkmal. Position: the Wikipedia list coordinate (50.07583, 8.77389) from the 1979 description; approximate. Alive: lifecheck NONE; Commons photo August 2020 and the current city route page (undated) describe it as standing; flagged for thin recent confirmation. Offenbach is a separate city, so this is a day-trip entry for Frankfurt.
